tldr: The authors propose RoboTok, a scalable data engine that takes a query demonstration video and rapidly indexes and retrieves demonstrations with similar 3D hand motion trajectories from massive web video collections. By learning a latent motion space from 3D hand trajectories expressed in an actor-centered frame, RoboTok accurately finds motion-matched videos without being misled by differences in viewpoint or scene appearance, substantially boosting the success rate of reinforcement learning for dexterous manipulation policies.
hero_caption: A t-SNE visualization of the latent motion space learned by RoboTok. Despite training purely on 3D hand trajectory alignment without any language labels or semantic annotations, clear clusters naturally emerge for distinct manipulation behaviors such as stirring in a bowl, cutting with a knife, and using a drill.
overview:
Teaching robots dexterous manipulation requires diverse and massive demonstration datasets. However, teleoperating physical robots to cover the long tail of real-world tasks is limited by both cost and practical feasibility. This has sparked growing interest in leveraging the endless human manipulation videos available on platforms like YouTube for robot learning. Yet, web videos present huge variations in camera viewpoint, scene background, lighting, and actor occlusions. More critically, there is a fundamental gap: visually similar clips often involve completely different hand movements, while identical hand motions can look entirely different visually.

To bridge this gap, the authors developed RoboTok, a data engine that retrieves task-relevant human demonstrations directly from web videos. The core insight is that representing 3D hand trajectories in an egocentric, actor-centered frame—rather than the camera frame—allows hand motions themselves to be compared invariant to viewpoint and background. The system reconstructs 3D hand poses from monocular video, estimates the actor's torso frame from wrist motion to normalize trajectories geometrically, and trains a lightweight encoder distilled from Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) trajectory alignment costs. This creates a compact latent motion space capable of fast vector nearest-neighbor search.

In evaluations across motion retrieval experiments on 100K web videos and external datasets, RoboTok decisively outperformed existing robot-data and video retrieval approaches. Furthermore, when hand poses extracted from retrieved videos were used to provide reward shaping for reinforcement learning (PPO) in simulation, policy success rates improved dramatically on challenging dexterous manipulation tasks with unconstrained wrist movement. This work demonstrates a scalable, continuous source of supervision from web video for robot learning.
contributions: Built RoboTok, the first internet-scale data engine to retrieve relevant human demonstrations from uncurated web video based on 3D hand trajectory alignment, bridging variations in camera viewpoint and visual appearance.

Proposed a framework that estimates an actor's static torso frame solely from wrist motion, geometrically normalizing 3D hand trajectories into an egocentric frame even when the actor's full body is not visible.
Distilled trajectory similarity from Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) into a lightweight encoder, enabling fast vector search and continuous indexing across massive video collections.

Incorporated hand poses from retrieved web demonstrations into hand-pose tracking rewards, substantially boosting policy learning speed and success rates on challenging simulated dexterous manipulation tasks.

sections.heading: Why Do We Need to Retrieve Hand Motions from Web Video?
sections.summary: To overcome the bottleneck of collecting real-world robot data, leveraging human web videos is promising. However, web videos vary widely in viewpoint and visual appearance, meaning visual similarity does not guarantee motion similarity. This paper proposes RoboTok, a data engine that resolves this retrieval challenge by learning representations based on actor-centered 3D hand trajectories.
sections.details:
Adapting robot learning to diverse real-world tasks and environments demands broad and varied demonstration data. Teleoperating physical robots to gather this data is prohibitively expensive, making it hard to cover the long tail of real-world scenarios. Consequently, demonstration retrieval from existing data pools has drawn significant attention.

Human videos on the web are especially appealing: they exist in volumes orders of magnitude larger than curated offline datasets and grow continuously every day. For humanoid robots and dexterous multi-fingered hands, human demonstrations are also morphologically well-aligned. However, using web video poses major hurdles. Beyond messy camera angles, environments, and occlusions, the core issue is that visual or semantic similarity does not imply similarity in hand manipulation behaviors. Two clips of an actor holding a kitchen knife may look alike, but the hand motion for chopping is entirely different from setting the knife down.

RoboTok tackles this challenge not by building a static dataset, but by functioning as a scalable engine that continuously indexes and retrieves web videos. Its key insight is that dexterous hand movements are only meaningful when represented relative to the actor or the manipulated object, rather than in the camera frame. By estimating the actor's torso frame from wrist motion and mapping viewpoint-invariant 3D hand trajectories into a latent motion space, RoboTok enables fast, accurate behavior retrieval at web scale.

sections.heading: Trends in Robot Learning Data and Demonstration Retrieval
sections.summary: The paper reviews prior work leveraging large-scale robot datasets and human videos, outlining the limitations of existing retrieval methods. Prior approaches largely depend on static robot datasets, 2D image-space motion, or semantic visual/language cues, whereas RoboTok sets itself apart by retrieving web-scale human videos purely based on 3D hand manipulation behaviors.
sections.details:
This section groups related prior research into three main areas:

### 2.1 Large-Scale Demonstration Data for Robot Learning
Large datasets such as Open X-Embodiment, DROID, and BridgeData V2 have driven recent progress in generalist robot foundation models. Methods like MimicGen also transform and augment existing trajectories. However, these systems still require dedicated robot infrastructure and curated engineering pipelines, limiting the variety of tasks they can cover. RoboTok taps into web-scale human video as a vast and continuously growing complementary data source.

### 2.2 Human Videos for Dexterous Manipulation Learning
Capitalizing on the morphological resemblance between human hands and multi-fingered robot hands, many works (such as VideoDex, EgoMimic, and CHORD) extract contact and motion representations from human manipulation to guide robots. Furthermore, large video corpora like HowTo100M and Action100M capture rich, natural human activities. However, discovering the exact motion clips needed for a given downstream task among millions of uncurated videos remained an open problem. RoboTok addresses this discovery bottleneck using egocentric 3D hand trajectories without relying on semantic labels or appearance.

### 2.3 Demonstration Retrieval for Robot Learning
Existing retrieval methods match state-action pairs, use Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with text prompts, leverage optical flow (FlowRetrieval), compute DTW on foundation model features (STRAP), or compare 2D hand paths (HAND). Yet these methods are constrained to static robot datasets or get biased by 2D image-space motion and visual semantics. RoboTok fundamentally differs by directly querying full web video collections using actor-centered 3D hand trajectories extracted from a query video.

sections.heading: How Do We Define Motion Similarity and Scale It Up?
sections.summary: This section defines the retrieval formulation for dexterous manipulation clips. Similarity across 3D trajectories of 21 hand joints is defined via Dynamic Time Warping (DTW), which serves as an oracle supervision signal to train a lightweight trajectory embedding model for fast, web-scale nearest-neighbor vector search.
sections.details:
Given a query video $q$ of a human performing a dexterous task and a candidate set of web video clips $\mathcal{D} = \{x_1, \ldots, x_N\}$, the goal is to retrieve the top-$K$ clips $\mathcal{R}_K(q; \mathcal{D})$ that share the most similar manipulation behaviors. Crucially, this similarity must reflect how the hands move over time rather than scene background or appearance.

To accommodate local variations in execution speed (e.g., chopping quickly versus slowly), the authors use Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) to align normalized 3D hand trajectories. For 21-joint hand pose trajectories $x_i, x_j$, the true similarity $s(q, i)$ is defined as the negative length-normalized cumulative Euclidean cost along the optimal alignment path $\pi$.

While retrieving the top-$K$ candidates based on this DTW metric is ideal, running exhaustive DTW pairwise comparisons against tens of thousands or millions of web clips at query time is computationally infeasible. To overcome this, the authors treat DTW as an oracle supervision signal and train an encoder $\Gamma$ that maps trajectories to a unit hypersphere $\mathbb{S}^{d-1}$. By training the inner product similarity $\langle \Gamma(x_i), \Gamma(x_j) \rangle$ to preserve DTW similarity rankings, the database can be pre-encoded offline, allowing inference to execute instantly via fast nearest-neighbor cosine similarity search.

sections.heading: Web Video Pipeline and Learning the Latent Motion Space
sections.summary: This section details the concrete architecture of RoboTok: candidate clip selection from web video, metric 3D hand pose estimation using WiLoR and MoGe-2, egocentric coordinate normalization estimating the torso from wrist motion, and training the lightweight encoder with DTW ranking losses.
sections.details:
RoboTok operates in two distinct phases: offline web video indexing and online query retrieval. The overall data processing and model pipeline proceeds as follows:

### 4.1 Training Data Pipeline
While web videos offer unmatched diversity, their heavy viewpoint changes and occlusions require robust preprocessing.
- **Clip Selection**: From the Action100M corpus, the authors automatically extract 4–8 second clips where the camera is nearly static (filtered via the Lucas-Kanade method), hands are visible, and at most one left and one right hand appear simultaneously.
- **Hand Pose Estimation and Metric Depth Reconstruction**: Using WiLoR at 5 fps, 21 3D hand keypoints are detected and tracked across frames. To resolve weak-perspective scale ambiguity, the monocular metric depth model MoGe-2 lifts keypoints to real-world metric 3D camera coordinates, with missing detections interpolated via HaWoR.
- **Acquiring an Egocentric Frame**: Trajectories expressed in camera coordinates cannot be compared across different viewpoints. To solve this, a lightweight network is trained to predict the actor's static torso frame (chest coordinate system) solely from wrist trajectory inputs. This normalizes trajectories into a shared body-centric frame whenever hands are visible, even if the actor's full torso is not in the frame.

### 4.2 RoboTok Model Architecture and Training Objectives
Because trajectories are already geometrically normalized, the model does not need to learn complex appearance invariances. The trajectory encoder is kept intentionally lightweight, consisting of per-frame positional encodings and cross-attention pooling that outputs an $\ell_2$-normalized $d$-dimensional embedding.
- **Batch Construction**: Across 100K clips, the probability that a random batch contains DTW-similar trajectories is near zero. To address this, the authors construct anchor-centered groups containing 2 positive examples from the oracle's top 20 and 1 hard negative sampled just outside the positive boundary, sharpening the encoder's discrimination near decision boundaries.
- **Loss Function**: To optimize retrieval quality directly, the model uses a combined loss: a set loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{set}}$ encouraging top neighbors to outscore boundary negatives, and a ranking loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rank}}$ aligning the relative order of positive pairs with their DTW ranks.
- **Inference**: Trajectories are pre-encoded into the index offline. At query time, retrieval requires only a single forward pass and a vector search. When new web videos arrive, they can be incrementally added to the index via forward encoding without retraining the model.

captions.F3: RoboTok training and inference workflow. Trajectories are encoded once offline into the latent motion space to build an index. At online inference, the query video is encoded similarly to instantly retrieve motion-matched clips via nearest-neighbor cosine similarity search.

sections.heading: Superior Retrieval Accuracy and Dramatic Gains in Robot RL
sections.summary: RoboTok was evaluated on retrieval precision across 100K Action100M clips and the external AssemblyHands dataset, as well as downstream RL policy performance in the VTDexManip simulation benchmark. RoboTok significantly outperformed existing baselines in retrieval and enabled guided robot policies to achieve massive success rate improvements on difficult tasks.
sections.details:
Evaluation focused on two fronts: quantitative and qualitative retrieval quality, and downstream robot policy learning using retrieved demonstrations.

### 5.1 Retrieval Quality Evaluation
Experiments were conducted on a 10,000-clip test set (from Action100M) and an external dataset with sensor-measured 3D ground truth, AssemblyHands (831 clips). RoboTok was compared against random selection, FlowRetrieval (optical flow), HAND (2D hand paths), and STRAP (DTW on foundation model features).
- **Results on RoboTok Corpus**: Retrieving the top 20 matches against the DTW oracle, the strongest baseline (STRAP) scored only mAP@20 = 0.007 and Recall@20 = 0.12, performing barely above chance. In contrast, RoboTok achieved mAP@20 = 0.353 and Recall@20 = 0.996, successfully recovering true motion neighbors on nearly every query. Its mean DTW cost reached 1.333 m, just 16% above the oracle's 1.145 m (compared to 4.776 m for random).
- **Generalization on AssemblyHands**: Under this domain shift, trends remained identical. RoboTok led all metrics with mAP@5 = 0.261 (vs. 0.133 for STRAP), confirming robust out-of-distribution generalization.

### 5.2 Evaluation on Downstream Robot Policies
To test whether retrieved videos effectively guide robot learning, the authors used the multi-fingered hand simulation benchmark VTDexManip. Because baseline performance had saturated under standard benchmark settings, the authors introduced a more realistic, harder exploration setup by removing wrist 3D translation constraints and eliminating dense reward shaping.
- **Tasks and RL Setup**: Three tasks were evaluated: BottleCap Turning, Faucet Screwing, and Lever Sliding. Using PPO, policies received a potential-based reward shaping term computed from distance to the retrieved demonstration hand-pose set, alongside task rewards. Demonstrations provided pose guidance only, without robot action labels or full trajectories.
- **Results**: On these challenging tasks, RoboTok-guided demonstrations dominated baselines. Across unseen object instances, RoboTok achieved success rates of 77.3% on BottleCap Turning (next best HAND: 59.5%), 44.8% on Faucet Screwing (HAND: 6.8%), and 79.3% on Lever Sliding (HAND: 19.5%), outperforming competitors by up to roughly 60 percentage points. Accurately retrieving motion-relevant demonstrations drastically reduced wasteful exploration during reinforcement learning.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook
sections.summary: RoboTok establishes a scalable data engine for retrieving and utilizing dexterous manipulation behaviors from human web videos. By framing hand motions in an actor-centered 3D representation, it enables appearance-invariant motion retrieval, offering a viable route to break the data collection bottleneck in robot learning.
sections.details:
This work introduced RoboTok, a data engine that extracts dexterous manipulation behaviors from internet videos to fuel robot learning. By learning a latent motion space over 3D hand trajectories centered on the actor's torso, RoboTok demonstrates that motion-based retrieval can scale across massive web video collections despite variations in camera viewpoint, appearance, and occlusions.

Empirical results confirmed that RoboTok dramatically surpasses existing retrieval baselines and that its retrieved demonstrations accelerate and improve dexterous manipulation policy learning in simulation. Instead of relying solely on static, pre-collected robot datasets, this framework unlocks a path to continuously transform the flood of human videos posted online into rich training resources for robots.

Future work aims to extend the system to dynamic camera footage—such as third-person walking footage and egocentric wearable camera streams—further tearing down data collection barriers in robot learning.

takeaways: Visual similarity does not equal motion similarity: When leveraging web video for robot learning, retrieving clips via geometrically normalized 3D hand trajectories yields far more useful demonstrations than visual feature matching (VLMs or image embeddings).

Smart normalization from wrist to torso: Even when an actor's body is out of frame, estimating a static torso frame purely from 3D wrist motion allows videos shot from arbitrary camera angles to be normalized into a single egocentric coordinate system.

Scaling via DTW knowledge distillation: Using computationally expensive DTW trajectory alignments as an oracle to train a lightweight encoder with ranking losses enables both web-scale nearest-neighbor vector search and continuous index expansion.

Coarse human videos provide strong RL guidance: Even without robot action labels, incorporating coarse human hand poses into potential-based reward shaping dramatically narrows the difficult exploration space for multi-fingered robot hands.
limitations: Limited to static-camera clips (the current pipeline excludes clips with significant camera motion, such as dynamic egocentric or wearable camera footage).
Dependent on hand detection and depth estimation accuracy (heavy occlusions or failure modes in monocular hand pose and depth estimators can degrade trajectory quality).
Does not explicitly model hand-object contact or physical interaction dynamics, focusing purely on aligning hand joint trajectories.
